about: Analysis of Circuits and Devices is the Part IA Cambridge Engineering course on linear circuits, electronic devices and AC power, given in 2025-26 as 22 lectures in weeks 3-8 of Michaelmas Term and weeks 1-3 of Lent Term. Following the 2025-26 official objectives, it covers DC analysis and network theorems, AC analysis with complex impedance and resonance, amplifier models and Bode plots, the p-n junction diode, the MOSFET and its small-signal model, ideal operational amplifiers, and a separate block of lectures on AC power flow, power factor correction and single-phase transformers. It runs alongside the IEP practical exercises (called the Integrated Electronics Project on the 1P3 syllabus page and the Integrated Electrical Project on the Part IA experimental work page) and is examined in Part IA Paper 3 (Electrical and Information Engineering), a 3-hour paper (per the 2025-26 Part IA guide). Topics and order follow the 2025-26 course page; check the 2026-27 page and Moodle for any changes.

notes.body:
The course starts with the tools for analysing any linear circuit. Everything later, including amplifiers and AC circuits, reuses them.

Basic elements
- Ohm's law for a resistor: V = IR. Power dissipated P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
- Ideal voltage source: keeps a fixed voltage across its terminals whatever current flows. A real source is modelled as an ideal source in series with an internal resistance.
- Ideal current source: drives a fixed current whatever the voltage across it. A real one has a large resistance in parallel.
- Resistors in series add: R = R₁ + R₂. In parallel, conductances add: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, so two in parallel give R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
- Potential divider: across R₂ in a series pair, V₂ = V × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Current divider: in two parallel resistors, I₂ = I × R₁/(R₁ + R₂).

Kirchhoff's laws
- Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the currents into any node sum to zero (charge is conserved).
- Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL): the voltages around any closed loop sum to zero (energy per unit charge is conserved).

Nodal analysis
- Choose a reference (earth) node. Label the unknown node voltages.
- At each unknown node, write KCL with each branch current expressed as (voltage difference)/resistance.
- Solve the simultaneous equations. Best when the circuit has few nodes or contains current sources.

Mesh analysis
- Assign a circulating current to each mesh (window) of a planar circuit.
- Write KVL round each mesh; a resistor shared by two meshes carries the difference of their currents.
- Best when the circuit has few meshes or contains voltage sources in series with resistors.

Worked nodal example
A 10 V source feeds node A through 2 Ω. A 4 Ω resistor joins A to earth. A 5 V source feeds A through another 4 Ω. KCL at A: (V_A − 10)/2 + V_A/4 + (V_A − 5)/4 = 0. Multiplying by 4: 2V_A − 20 + V_A + V_A − 5 = 0, so V_A = 25/4 = 6.25 V. The current in the earthed 4 Ω resistor is 1.56 A.

Good habits
- Mark reference directions for currents and polarities for voltages before writing equations. A negative answer simply means the real direction is opposite.
- Count unknowns and equations; they must match.
- Check the answer with a different method (for instance superposition) or by verifying KCL at another node.

Exam tips: choose nodal or mesh analysis by counting which gives fewer equations, and show the equations clearly; method marks are usually available even if the arithmetic slips.

notes.h: Thévenin and Norton equivalents, superposition and power transfer
notes.body:
These theorems let you replace a complicated linear network by something simple, so you can see at once how it behaves with any load.

Superposition
- In a linear circuit with several independent sources, the response (any voltage or current) is the sum of the responses to each source acting alone.
- To switch off a source: replace an ideal voltage source by a short circuit, and an ideal current source by an open circuit.
- Superposition works for voltages and currents, not for power (power is quadratic).
- Check of the nodal example (10 V via 2 Ω, 5 V via 4 Ω, 4 Ω to earth): the 10 V source alone gives 10 × 2/(2 + 2) = 5 V, since the other two 4 Ω resistors are in parallel (2 Ω). The 5 V source alone gives 5 × (4/3)/(4/3 + 4) = 1.25 V. Total 6.25 V, as before.

Thévenin's theorem
- Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by an ideal voltage source V_Th in series with a resistance R_Th.
- V_Th is the open-circuit voltage at the terminals.
- R_Th is the resistance seen looking into the terminals with all independent sources switched off. Equivalently R_Th = V_oc/I_sc, where I_sc is the short-circuit current.

Norton's theorem
- The same network can be replaced by an ideal current source I_N in parallel with R_N.
- I_N is the short-circuit current, and R_N = R_Th. The two forms are related by V_Th = I_N R_Th (source transformation).

Worked example
A 12 V source in series with 4 kΩ, with 12 kΩ across the output terminals.
- V_Th = 12 × 12/(4 + 12) = 9 V.
- R_Th = 4 kΩ ∥ 12 kΩ = 3 kΩ.
- Norton: I_N = 9/3 = 3 mA (which is also 12 V/4 kΩ, the short-circuit current).

Maximum power transfer
- A load R_L on a Thévenin source receives P = V_Th² R_L/(R_Th + R_L)².
- Differentiating, P is greatest when R_L = R_Th, giving P_max = V_Th²/(4R_Th).
- In the example, a 3 kΩ load receives 81/(4 × 3000) = 6.75 mW.
- At maximum power transfer only 50% of the power produced by the source reaches the load. Power systems therefore do not operate there; they aim for high efficiency with R_L ≫ R_Th. Matching matters in signal circuits where the source power is small.
- For AC sources with internal impedance Z_Th, maximum power is delivered when Z_L is the complex conjugate of Z_Th.

Why this matters later
- An amplifier's input looks like a resistance R_in, and its output looks like a Thévenin source with output resistance R_out. Loading calculations for amplifiers are just Thévenin calculations.

Exam tips: always state how you found R_Th (sources switched off, or V_oc/I_sc), and remember that dependent sources must be left on when finding R_Th.

notes.h: AC circuits: phasors, complex impedance and r.m.s. values
notes.body:
With sinusoidal sources, every voltage and current in a linear circuit is a sinusoid at the same frequency. Complex numbers turn the differential equations into the same algebra as DC analysis.

Phasors
- A sinusoid v(t) = V_m cos(ωt + φ) is represented by the complex number V = V_m e^(jφ) (engineers write j for √−1). Then v(t) = Re(V e^(jωt)).
- Phasors are often scaled to r.m.s. magnitude instead of peak; be consistent within a problem.
- Differentiation becomes multiplication by jω, so a phase lead of 90°.

Impedance
- Resistor: Z = R (voltage and current in phase).
- Inductor: v = L di/dt gives Z = jωL (current lags voltage by 90°). Its reactance X_L = ωL.
- Capacitor: i = C dv/dt gives Z = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC) (current leads voltage by 90°). Reactance magnitude 1/(ωC).
- Ohm's law V = ZI, KCL, KVL, series and parallel rules, dividers, nodal and mesh analysis, Thévenin and Norton all carry over with complex impedances.
- Admittance Y = 1/Z is convenient for parallel branches.

Worked example
A 100 Ω resistor in series with a 0.5 H inductor on a 230 V r.m.s., 50 Hz supply.
- X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.5 ≈ 157 Ω, so Z = 100 + j157 Ω.
- |Z| = √(100² + 157²) ≈ 186 Ω and arg Z = arctan(157/100) ≈ 57.5°.
- I = 230/186 ≈ 1.24 A r.m.s., lagging the voltage by 57.5°.

Frequency-dependent circuits
- An RC potential divider with output across C has V_out/V_in = 1/(1 + jωCR): a low-pass filter whose gain falls to 1/√2 at ω = 1/(CR).
- With output across R it becomes jωCR/(1 + jωCR): a high-pass filter.
- So impedance analysis leads straight to frequency response and gain.

R.m.s. values and power in resistive loads
- The r.m.s. value is the square root of the mean of the square over a period. It is the DC value that would deliver the same average power to a resistor.
- For a sinusoid, V_rms = V_m/√2 ≈ 0.707V_m. UK mains is quoted as 230 V r.m.s., so its peak is about 325 V.
- Average power in a resistor: P = V_rms I_rms = V_rms²/R.
- For reactive loads the average power also depends on the phase angle; that is developed in the AC power lectures.

Exam tips: convert to complex form once, do all the algebra with complex numbers, and only take modulus and argument at the end; always state whether phasors are peak or r.m.s.

notes.h: RLC circuits, resonance and Q factor
notes.body:
When inductance and capacitance appear together, their reactances can cancel at one frequency. This resonance is used in tuned circuits and filters, and it mirrors the mechanical resonance met in 1P1 Mechanical Vibrations.

Series RLC circuit
- Z = R + j(ωL − 1/(ωC)).
- At the resonant frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC), the reactances cancel, so Z = R: the impedance is a minimum and purely resistive, the current is a maximum and in phase with the source voltage.
- Below ω₀ the circuit is capacitive (current leads); above ω₀ it is inductive (current lags).

Quality factor
- Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR) = (1/R)√(L/C) for the series circuit.
- At resonance the voltages across L and across C are each Q times the source voltage, in antiphase, so they cancel. With high Q these voltages can be far larger than the supply, which matters for component ratings.
- Q also measures sharpness: the half-power (−3 dB) bandwidth is Δω = ω₀/Q = R/L for the series circuit.
- Q can be read as 2π × (peak energy stored)/(energy dissipated per cycle).

Worked example
L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF, R = 10 Ω in series.
- ω₀ = 1/√(10⁻² × 10⁻⁷) = 1/√(10⁻⁹) ≈ 31,600 rad/s, so f₀ ≈ 5.03 kHz.
- Q = ω₀L/R = 316/10 ≈ 31.6.
- Bandwidth = R/L = 1000 rad/s ≈ 159 Hz.
- With 1 V at resonance, the current is 0.1 A and the inductor and capacitor each carry about 31.6 V.

Parallel RLC circuit
- For R, L and C all in parallel, the admittance is Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)).
- At ω₀ = 1/√(LC) the admittance is a minimum (impedance a maximum, equal to R) and the circuit draws the least current from a voltage source.
- Q = R/(ω₀L) = ω₀CR for the parallel circuit: a large parallel resistance means low losses and a sharp resonance.
- At resonance, a current Q times the supply current circulates between L and C.
- Real inductors have series resistance, so practical "parallel" tuned circuits differ slightly; the simple results above hold well for high Q.

Analogy with mechanical vibration
- Series RLC: L ↔ mass, R ↔ dashpot, 1/C ↔ spring stiffness. Q here corresponds to 1/(2ζ) in vibration.

Exam tips: identify series or parallel before quoting a Q formula, check the units of ω₀ (rad/s versus Hz), and sketch |Z| or |I| against frequency to show resonance and bandwidth.

An amplifier can be treated as a black box with a few parameters. This makes it easy to connect amplifiers to sources, loads and each other.

The amplifier model
- Input: a resistance R_in between the input terminals.
- Output: a Thévenin source with open-circuit voltage A_v0 v_in in series with an output resistance R_out.
- A_v0 is the open-circuit (unloaded) voltage gain.

Loading
- A source with internal resistance R_s driving the amplifier gives v_in = v_s R_in/(R_s + R_in).
- A load R_L gives v_out = A_v0 v_in R_L/(R_out + R_L).
- Overall gain v_out/v_s = [R_in/(R_s + R_in)] × A_v0 × [R_L/(R_out + R_L)].
- For a good voltage amplifier: R_in ≫ R_s and R_out ≪ R_L.
- Example: R_s = 1 kΩ, R_in = 9 kΩ, A_v0 = 100, R_out = 1 kΩ, R_L = 4 kΩ. Overall gain = 0.9 × 100 × 0.8 = 72.

Decibels
- Power gain in dB = 10 log₁₀(P_out/P_in).
- Voltage gain in dB = 20 log₁₀(V_out/V_in) (strictly when both are across equal resistances, but widely used for voltage ratios).
- A gain of 72 is 20 log₁₀ 72 ≈ 37.1 dB. Factors of 2, 10 and 1/√2 correspond to about +6 dB, +20 dB and −3 dB.

Multistage amplifiers and coupling
- In a cascade the gains multiply, so their dB values add, but each stage's R_in loads the previous stage's R_out. Include these loading factors.
- Coupling capacitors pass the signal but block DC, so stages can be biased independently. They make the gain fall at low frequency.

Frequency response and bandwidth
- Gain is usually flat over a middle range (the mid-band gain) and falls at low and high frequency.
- The bandwidth is the range between the lower and upper −3 dB (half-power) frequencies.
- A coupling capacitor C feeding a total resistance R forms a high-pass section with corner ω = 1/(RC). Stray and device capacitances form low-pass sections at high frequency.

Bode plots
- Plot gain in dB and phase against log frequency.
- A single low-pass section 1/(1 + jω/ω_c) is flat below ω_c, −3 dB at ω_c, then falls at 20 dB per decade. Its phase goes from 0 to −90°, passing −45° at ω_c.
- A high-pass section jω/ω_c/(1 + jω/ω_c) rises at 20 dB per decade below ω_c and is flat above; its phase goes from +90° to 0.
- Straight-line asymptotes make sketching quick; for products of sections, add dB and add phases.

Exam tips: draw the model with R_s and R_L explicitly, write the two divider factors, and convert to dB only at the end.

notes.h: Semiconductors and the p-n junction diode
notes.body:
Electronic devices depend on controlling the number and type of charge carriers in a semiconductor, usually silicon.

Intrinsic silicon
- Each silicon atom has four valence electrons forming covalent bonds with neighbours. At room temperature a few bonds break thermally, giving free electrons and the vacancies they leave, called holes. A hole behaves like a mobile positive charge.
- In pure (intrinsic) silicon, electron and hole concentrations are equal (n = p = nᵢ), and nᵢ rises steeply with temperature.

Doping
- n-type: add a small amount of a group V element (such as phosphorus or arsenic). Each donor atom has a fifth electron that is easily freed, so electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers.
- p-type: add a group III element (such as boron). Each acceptor atom accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, creating a hole; holes are the majority carriers.
- In equilibrium np = nᵢ², so increasing one carrier type reduces the other.
- Doping changes conductivity by many orders of magnitude and lets engineers choose it.

Current flow
- Drift: carriers move under an electric field.
- Diffusion: carriers move from high to low concentration. Both matter in devices.

The p-n junction
- When p- and n-type regions meet, holes diffuse into the n side and electrons into the p side, where they recombine. This leaves a depletion region near the junction that has no mobile carriers but contains fixed ionised dopant atoms: negative on the p side, positive on the n side.
- These fixed charges set up an electric field and a built-in potential barrier that stops further net diffusion in equilibrium.
- Forward bias (p side positive): the barrier is lowered and carriers diffuse across in large numbers, so the current rises exponentially with voltage.
- Reverse bias (p side negative): the barrier and depletion region grow; only a tiny reverse saturation current of minority carriers flows, until breakdown at a large reverse voltage (used deliberately in Zener diodes).

The diode equation
- I = I_s[exp(V/(nV_T)) − 1], where I_s is the reverse saturation current, n is an ideality factor (between 1 and 2), and V_T = kT/q is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV at room temperature.
- With n = 1, the current increases about tenfold for every 60 mV of forward bias.
- For hand calculations a silicon diode is often modelled as an ideal switch with a constant forward drop of about 0.6 to 0.7 V.
- Example: a 5 V supply, 1 kΩ resistor and silicon diode in series: I ≈ (5 − 0.7)/1000 = 4.3 mA.
- Small-signal resistance: r_d = nV_T/I, about 26 Ω at 1 mA for n = 1.

Exam tips: be able to sketch the I–V characteristic with both bias regions labelled, and explain the depletion region in terms of fixed and mobile charges.

notes.h: The MOSFET: operation, DC characteristics and the load line
notes.body:
The metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) is the device in almost all modern integrated circuits. 1P3 focuses on the n-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET.

Structure and principle
- Two heavily doped n-type regions (source and drain) sit in a p-type body. The gate is a conductor separated from the body by a thin insulating oxide.
- With no gate voltage, the source and drain are separated by p-type material (two back-to-back junctions), so no current flows.
- A positive gate–source voltage V_GS attracts electrons to the surface under the gate. Above the threshold voltage V_T, an inverted n-type channel forms, connecting source and drain.
- The gate is insulated, so it draws essentially no DC current: the input resistance is very high. The device is controlled by voltage, with the field from the gate setting the channel's conductivity.

Regions of operation (square-law model)
- Cut-off: V_GS < V_T, so I_D ≈ 0.
- Triode (ohmic) region: V_GS > V_T and V_DS < V_GS − V_T. The channel behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor: I_D = K[2(V_GS − V_T)V_DS − V_DS²].
- Saturation region: V_GS > V_T and V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T. The channel pinches off at the drain end and the current is nearly independent of V_DS: I_D = K(V_GS − V_T)².
- K depends on the device geometry and materials. Notation varies between textbooks and lecture notes (some write K as ½k′(W/L), others put a factor ½ in front of the bracket), so use the form your lecturer gives. The two expressions for I_D agree at V_DS = V_GS − V_T.
- Here V_T means the MOSFET threshold voltage; do not confuse it with the thermal voltage kT/q in the diode equation, which some texts also call V_T.
- In practice I_D rises slowly with V_DS in saturation (channel-length modulation), giving a finite output resistance.
- Amplifiers use the saturation region; digital switches use cut-off and triode.

Characteristics
- Output characteristics: I_D against V_DS for several values of V_GS. Each curve rises (triode) then levels off (saturation).
- Transfer characteristic: I_D against V_GS in saturation, a parabola starting at V_T.

Load line and operating point
- In a common-source stage, the drain connects to V_DD through R_D and the source to earth. KVL gives V_DS = V_DD − I_D R_D, a straight load line on the output characteristics, from (V_DD, 0) to (0, V_DD/R_D).
- The operating (quiescent) point is where the load line meets the curve for the chosen V_GS.
- Example: V_DD = 15 V, R_D = 2 kΩ, K = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V, V_GS = 3 V. Then I_D = 1 × (3 − 1)² = 4 mA and V_DS = 15 − 8 = 7 V. Since 7 V ≥ V_GS − V_T = 2 V, the assumption of saturation is valid.
- As V_GS swings with a signal, the operating point moves along the load line. Graphically this shows the gain and the limits of output swing (cut-off at one end, entry into triode at the other).
- Gate bias is usually set with a potential divider from V_DD, because the gate takes no DC current.

Exam tips: always check which region you are in after calculating I_D, and draw the load line with both intercepts labelled.

notes.h: Small-signal MOSFET model and the common-source amplifier
notes.body:
For small signals about the operating point, the curved MOSFET characteristics can be replaced by straight lines. This gives a linear equivalent circuit that can be analysed with the ordinary circuit methods.

Linearising
- Write each quantity as a DC bias plus a small signal: v_GS = V_GS + v_gs, i_D = I_D + i_d.
- For small signals, i_d = g_m v_gs + v_ds/r_ds.
- Transconductance g_m = ∂I_D/∂V_GS at the operating point. With I_D = K(V_GS − V_T)², g_m = 2K(V_GS − V_T) = 2√(K I_D) = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T).
- Output resistance r_ds = ∂V_DS/∂I_D (from the slope of the output characteristic in saturation). It is large; if not given, treat it as infinite.

Small-signal equivalent circuit
- Gate to source: an open circuit (no gate current).
- Drain to source: a dependent current source g_m v_gs in parallel with r_ds.
- DC supplies become signal earth (a constant voltage has no signal component). Large coupling and bypass capacitors become short circuits at mid-band frequencies.

The common-source amplifier
- Input to the gate, output from the drain, source common (earthed for signals).
- With drain resistor R_D and load R_L, the output node sees r_ds ∥ R_D ∥ R_L, so v_out = −g_m v_gs (r_ds ∥ R_D ∥ R_L).
- Mid-band voltage gain A_v = −g_m(r_ds ∥ R_D ∥ R_L). The minus sign means the output is inverted (180° phase shift).
- Input resistance is set by the gate bias network (for a potential divider, R_G1 ∥ R_G2), typically hundreds of kΩ.
- Output resistance is r_ds ∥ R_D.
- Example: K = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V, V_GS = 3 V gives I_D = 4 mA and g_m = 4 mA/V. With R_D = 2 kΩ and r_ds very large, A_v = −8. If r_ds = 50 kΩ, R_D ∥ r_ds ≈ 1.92 kΩ and A_v ≈ −7.7.

Source resistor
- A resistor R_S in the source lead stabilises the bias against variations in V_T and K. If it is not bypassed by a capacitor, the gain falls to about −g_m R_D/(1 + g_m R_S) (with r_ds infinite). Bypassing R_S with a capacitor restores the full gain at signal frequencies while keeping DC stability.

Frequency effects
- Input and output coupling capacitors form high-pass sections with the resistances they see, setting the lower −3 dB frequency. Internal device capacitances set the upper limit.

Limits of the model
- It holds only for small signals. Large swings reach cut-off or the triode region and distort the output; the load line shows where.

Exam tips: always find the DC operating point first (and check saturation), then compute g_m, then draw the small-signal circuit with supplies earthed and capacitors shorted.

An operational amplifier (op-amp) is a high-gain differential amplifier made as an integrated circuit. With negative feedback it becomes a precise, predictable building block whose behaviour depends almost only on external resistors.

The ideal op-amp
- Output v_out = A(v₊ − v₋), with open-loop gain A → ∞.
- Infinite input resistance (no current into the inputs) and zero output resistance.
- With negative feedback (output connected back to the inverting input), the output adjusts so that v₊ = v₋ (the "virtual short"), while still no current flows into either input.

Standard circuits (ideal analysis)
- Inverting amplifier: input through R₁ to v₋, feedback R_f from output to v₋, v₊ earthed. v₋ is a virtual earth, so v_in/R₁ = −v_out/R_f and gain = −R_f/R₁. Input resistance = R₁.
- Non-inverting amplifier: input to v₊, feedback divider R_f and R₁ from output to earth with the tap at v₋. Gain = 1 + R_f/R₁. Input resistance is very high.
- Voltage follower (buffer): output joined to v₋, input to v₊. Gain 1, very high input resistance and very low output resistance; used to stop loading.
- Summing amplifier: several inputs through R₁, R₂, … to a virtual-earth node: v_out = −R_f(v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂ + …).
- Difference amplifier: with matching resistor ratios, v_out = (R₂/R₁)(v₂ − v₁), where v₂ is applied (via a divider) to the non-inverting input and v₁ to the inverting input.
- Integrator: replace R_f by capacitor C: v_out = −(1/RC)∫v_in dt; in the frequency domain, gain = −1/(jωCR).

Worked example
- Inverting stage, R₁ = 10 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ: gain −10, input resistance 10 kΩ.
- Non-inverting stage with the same resistors: gain 1 + 10 = 11.

Finite gain and feedback
- With finite A, the non-inverting gain is A/(1 + Aβ), where β = R₁/(R₁ + R_f) is the fraction of the output fed back. If Aβ ≫ 1, this tends to 1/β = 1 + R_f/R₁, independent of A. This is the key benefit of negative feedback: precise gain from imprecise, high-gain devices.
- Example: A = 10⁵ and β = 1/11 give gain ≈ 10.9988, only about 0.011% below 11.

Practical limits
- The output cannot exceed the supply rails; beyond that it saturates (clips).
- Open-loop gain falls with frequency. For many op-amps the gain–bandwidth product is roughly constant, so a higher closed-loop gain means a lower bandwidth.
- Other limits include slew rate (maximum rate of change of output), input offset voltage and input bias currents.

Exam tips: state the two ideal rules (no input current, v₊ = v₋ with negative feedback) and apply KCL at the inverting input; that solves almost every op-amp circuit.

notes.h: AC power: real, reactive and apparent power
notes.body:
In AC power systems, voltage and current are generally out of phase, so the product of r.m.s. voltage and current is not the power consumed. This section explains the three kinds of "power" and how to correct a poor power factor.

Definitions (r.m.s. quantities, current lagging voltage by φ)
- Real (active) power P = VI cos φ, in watts (W). This is the average power actually converted into heat or work.
- Reactive power Q = VI sin φ, in volt-amperes reactive (VAr). It represents energy that surges back and forth between source and the load's inductance or capacitance each cycle, with zero average.
- Apparent power S = VI, in volt-amperes (VA). It sets the current and so the size of cables, transformers and generators.
- Complex power S = V I* = P + jQ, where I* is the complex conjugate of the current phasor. With this convention an inductive load (current lagging) absorbs positive Q, and a capacitor generates reactive power (negative Q).
- Power triangle: S² = P² + Q², and power factor = P/S = cos φ, described as lagging (inductive) or leading (capacitive).

Using P and Q to solve circuits
- Real powers add and reactive powers add, for loads connected in series or in parallel. Apparent powers do not simply add.
- Example: on a 230 V supply, load A takes 2 kW at unity power factor; load B takes 3 kVA at 0.6 lagging, i.e. 1.8 kW and 2.4 kVAr. Total P = 3.8 kW, Q = 2.4 kVAr, S = √(3.8² + 2.4²) ≈ 4.49 kVA, power factor ≈ 0.85 lagging, supply current ≈ 4494/230 ≈ 19.5 A.
- For a pure reactance X carrying current I: Q = I²X. For a resistance: P = I²R.

Why power factor matters
- For the same real power, a low power factor means a larger current. Larger current means bigger I²R losses in cables and bigger voltage drops, and equipment must be rated for the extra VA. Suppliers therefore penalise large industrial users with poor power factor.

Power factor correction
- Most industrial loads (induction motors) are inductive. Connecting a capacitor in parallel supplies some or all of the reactive power locally: a capacitor across V supplies Q_C = V²ωC.
- The real power is unchanged; the supply current falls.
- Worked example: a load takes 10 A from 230 V, 50 Hz at 0.8 lagging. S = 2300 VA, P = 1840 W, Q = 1380 VAr. For unity power factor: C = 1380/(230² × 2π × 50) ≈ 83 µF. The supply current falls to 1840/230 = 8 A.
- Correcting only to 0.95 lagging leaves Q = 1840 tan(cos⁻¹ 0.95) ≈ 605 VAr, so only about 775 VAr (C ≈ 47 µF) is needed. Full correction to unity is often not economic.

Exam tips: draw the power triangle, keep track of the signs of Q, add P and Q separately, and only then find S, power factor and current.

Transformers change AC voltage levels with very high efficiency. They make long-distance power transmission practical and are found in almost every electronic power supply.

Principle of operation
- Two coils (primary N₁ turns, secondary N₂ turns) are wound on a common laminated iron core.
- An alternating primary voltage drives an alternating magnetic flux Φ round the core. By Faraday's law, the flux induces an emf in each turn: e = N dΦ/dt.
- Because both coils link the same flux, the emf per turn is the same: V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂ (ideal transformer).
- For sinusoidal flux of peak Φ_m at frequency f, the r.m.s. emf is E = 4.44 f N Φ_m. Example: 230 V at 50 Hz with Φ_m = 2 mWb needs N ≈ 230/(4.44 × 50 × 0.002) ≈ 518 turns.

The ideal transformer
- No losses, no leakage flux, and an infinitely permeable core needing no magnetising current.
- Power in equals power out, so I₁/I₂ = N₂/N₁: a step-down transformer gives a larger secondary current.
- Impedance referral: a load Z_L on the secondary appears at the primary as (N₁/N₂)² Z_L. Example: 2 Ω on the secondary of a 10:1 step-down transformer looks like 200 Ω from the primary. Transformers can therefore be used to match impedances.

The real transformer and its equivalent circuit
- Winding resistances R₁ and R₂ cause copper (I²R) losses that depend on load.
- Leakage flux that links only one winding is represented by leakage reactances X₁ and X₂ in series with each winding.
- A real core needs a magnetising current to set up the flux: represented by a magnetising reactance X_m in a shunt branch.
- Hysteresis and eddy currents in the core cause core (iron) losses: represented by a resistance R_c in parallel with X_m. Laminating the core reduces eddy currents.
- Referring all secondary quantities to the primary (multiplying impedances by (N₁/N₂)², voltages by N₁/N₂ and currents by N₂/N₁) gives a single circuit. In the approximate equivalent circuit, the shunt branch is moved to the input terminals so the series parts combine into R_eq and X_eq.

Finding the parameters
- Open-circuit test: rated voltage on one winding, the other open. The current is small, so the measured power is almost all core loss; gives R_c and X_m.
- Short-circuit test: one winding shorted, a reduced voltage applied to drive rated current. The flux is small, so the measured power is almost all copper loss; gives R_eq and X_eq.

Efficiency
- Efficiency = output/(output + core loss + copper loss). Core loss is roughly constant; copper loss varies with the square of load current.
- Efficiency is greatest at the load where copper loss equals core loss.
- Example: a 10 kVA transformer with 100 W core loss and 200 W full-load copper loss has 10/10.3 ≈ 97.1% efficiency at full load and unity power factor. Maximum efficiency is at √(100/200) ≈ 0.71 of full load (about 7.07 kVA), where it is about 97.2%.

Exam tips: state the assumptions of the ideal transformer, refer everything to one side before calculating, and label the equivalent circuit elements with what physical effect each represents.

questions.q: A 12 V source is connected across 4 kΩ and 2 kΩ in series. What is the voltage across the 2 kΩ resistor?
questions.why: Potential divider: 12 × 2/(4 + 2) = 4 V. 8 V is across the 4 kΩ resistor; 6 V assumes equal resistors; 2 V is the circuit current, 12/(4 + 2) = 2 mA, mistaken for a voltage.

questions.q: Node A is fed by 10 V through 2 Ω and by 5 V through 4 Ω, and is joined to earth by 4 Ω. What is V_A?
questions.why: KCL: (V_A − 10)/2 + V_A/4 + (V_A − 5)/4 = 0 gives 4V_A = 25, so V_A = 6.25 V. 7.5 V is the mean of the two sources; 5.0 V is the contribution of the 10 V source alone; 3.75 V results from a sign error on the 5 V branch.

questions.q: Using mesh analysis, find the current in each resistor of this circuit: a 10 V source in series with 2 Ω forms the left branch, a 4 Ω resistor forms the middle branch, and a 5 V source in series with 4 Ω forms the right branch, all three branches connected between the same two nodes (both sources have their positive terminals at the top node). Check your answer against nodal analysis.
markScheme: Defines two mesh currents, I₁ (left window) and I₂ (right window), clockwise
Left mesh KVL: 10 = 2I₁ + 4(I₁ − I₂), i.e. 6I₁ − 4I₂ = 10
Right mesh KVL: −5 = 4(I₂ − I₁) + 4I₂, i.e. −4I₁ + 8I₂ = −5
Solves I₁ = 1.875 A, I₂ = 0.3125 A; middle resistor carries I₁ − I₂ = 1.5625 A downwards
Check: top node voltage = 4 × 1.5625 = 6.25 V, agreeing with nodal analysis
questions.modelAnswer: Take clockwise mesh currents I₁ in the left window and I₂ in the right window. Left mesh: going up through the 10 V source gives a rise of 10 V; the drops are 2I₁ in the 2 Ω resistor and 4(I₁ − I₂) in the shared 4 Ω resistor, so 10 = 6I₁ − 4I₂. Right mesh: going up through the shared resistor gives a drop of 4(I₂ − I₁); going down the right branch gives a drop of 4I₂ in the 4 Ω resistor and a further drop of 5 V because the source is entered at its positive terminal. So 0 = −4(I₂ − I₁) − 4I₂ − 5, i.e. −4I₁ + 8I₂ = −5. From the first equation I₁ = (10 + 4I₂)/6. Substituting and multiplying by 6: −40 − 16I₂ + 48I₂ = −30, so I₂ = 10/32 = 0.3125 A and I₁ = (10 + 1.25)/6 = 1.875 A. So the 2 Ω resistor carries 1.875 A (up through the 10 V source), the middle 4 Ω carries I₁ − I₂ = 1.5625 A downwards, and the right-hand 4 Ω carries 0.3125 A downwards, flowing into the positive terminal of the 5 V source (that source is absorbing power). The top node is at 4 × 1.5625 = 6.25 V, matching the nodal result, and (6.25 − 5)/4 = 0.3125 A confirms the right-hand branch current.

questions.q: A 12 V source in series with 4 kΩ has 12 kΩ connected across its output terminals. What is the Thévenin equivalent seen at the terminals?
questions.why: V_Th is the open-circuit voltage 12 × 12/16 = 9 V. R_Th is 4 kΩ ∥ 12 kΩ = 3 kΩ with the source shorted. 16 kΩ adds the resistors in series, which is wrong because the source is replaced by a short; 12 V ignores the divider.

questions.q: A source with Thévenin equivalent 9 V and 3 kΩ feeds a variable load resistor. What is the maximum power the load can receive?
questions.why: Maximum power occurs at R_L = R_Th = 3 kΩ: P = V_Th²/(4R_Th) = 81/12,000 = 6.75 mW. 27 mW is V²/R (short-circuit power in R_Th); 13.5 mW uses V_Th²/(2R_Th) instead of V_Th²/(4R_Th); 3.0 mW is the short-circuit current I_N = 9/3 = 3 mA mistaken for a power.

questions.q: Use superposition to find the voltage at node A in a circuit where a 10 V source feeds A through 2 Ω, a 5 V source feeds A through 4 Ω, and a 4 Ω resistor connects A to earth. Then find the Thévenin equivalent seen by the earthed 4 Ω resistor.
markScheme: 10 V alone (5 V shorted): the two 4 Ω in parallel = 2 Ω, so V_A = 10 × 2/4 = 5 V
Total V_A = 6.25 V
Remove the earthed 4 Ω: R_Th = 2 ∥ 4 = 4/3 Ω; V_Th from divider = 5 + (10 − 5) × 4/6 = 8.33 V
questions.modelAnswer: With the 10 V source alone (5 V source shorted), the 4 Ω to earth and the 4 Ω to the shorted source are in parallel, giving 2 Ω, so V_A = 10 × 2/(2 + 2) = 5 V. With the 5 V source alone (10 V source shorted), the 2 Ω and earthed 4 Ω are in parallel, giving 4/3 Ω, so V_A = 5 × (4/3)/(4/3 + 4) = 1.25 V. By superposition V_A = 6.25 V. For the Thévenin equivalent seen by the earthed 4 Ω resistor, remove it: with both sources switched off, R_Th = 2 Ω ∥ 4 Ω = 4/3 Ω. The open-circuit voltage: current (10 − 5)/(2 + 4) = 0.833 A flows from the 10 V source to the 5 V source, so V_Th = 10 − 2 × 0.833 = 8.33 V. Reconnecting the 4 Ω load: 8.33 × 4/(4 + 1.333) = 6.25 V, agreeing with the superposition result.

questions.q: A series RLC circuit has L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF and R = 10 Ω. What are its resonant frequency and Q?

questions.q: At resonance, what is the impedance of a series RLC circuit?

questions.q: A series RLC circuit (L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF, R = 10 Ω) is driven by 1 V r.m.s. at its resonant frequency. Find the current, the voltage across the capacitor, and the half-power bandwidth. Explain why a high-Q circuit is selective.
markScheme: At resonance Z = R = 10 Ω, so I = 0.1 A r.m.s.
Bandwidth Δω = R/L = 1000 rad/s ≈ 159 Hz
Q = ω₀/Δω ≈ 31.6
High Q: response falls off sharply away from ω₀, so only a narrow band of frequencies produces a large current
questions.modelAnswer: At resonance the reactances cancel, so the impedance is just R = 10 Ω and the current is 1/10 = 0.1 A r.m.s., in phase with the supply. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) ≈ 31,623 rad/s. The capacitor voltage is I/(ω₀C) = 0.1/(31,623 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 31.6 V, which is Q times the supply voltage (Q = ω₀L/R ≈ 31.6); the inductor voltage is the same size but in antiphase. The half-power bandwidth is R/L = 10/0.01 = 1000 rad/s, about 159 Hz. A high-Q circuit is selective because its impedance rises steeply as the frequency moves away from ω₀, so only signals within the narrow bandwidth around ω₀ produce a large current; this is how tuned circuits pick out one frequency.

questions.q: An amplifier has R_in = 9 kΩ, open-circuit gain 100 and R_out = 1 kΩ. It is driven from a source with 1 kΩ internal resistance and feeds a 4 kΩ load. What is the overall voltage gain v_out/v_s?
questions.why: Gain = [9/(1 + 9)] × 100 × [4/(1 + 4)] = 0.9 × 100 × 0.8 = 72. 100 ignores loading at both ends; 90 includes only input loading; 80 includes only output loading.

questions.q: A voltage gain of 100 corresponds to how many decibels?
questions.why: Voltage gain in dB = 20 log₁₀(100) = 40 dB. 20 dB is a gain of 10 (or the result of wrongly using 10 log₁₀ for a voltage ratio); 100 dB copies the ratio as if it were already in decibels; 10 dB is 10 log₁₀ 10, i.e. a power ratio of 10, not a voltage ratio of 100.

questions.q: Two identical amplifier stages, each with R_in = 10 kΩ, open-circuit gain 20 and R_out = 2 kΩ, are cascaded. They are driven from an ideal voltage source and the second stage drives a 10 kΩ load. Find the overall voltage gain in absolute terms and in dB, and explain why it is less than 20 × 20.
markScheme: Ideal source, so first stage input = v_s
Interstage loading: second stage R_in (10 kΩ) loads first stage R_out (2 kΩ): factor 10/12 = 0.833
Output loading: 10/(2 + 10) = 0.833
In dB: 20 log₁₀ 278 ≈ 48.9 dB, versus 52 dB without loading; the difference is the voltage lost across each R_out
questions.modelAnswer: The source is ideal, so the full v_s appears at the first stage input. The first stage produces an open-circuit voltage 20v_s, but its 2 kΩ output resistance forms a divider with the second stage's 10 kΩ input resistance, so the second stage receives 20v_s × 10/12 = 16.67v_s. The second stage produces 20 × 16.67v_s = 333v_s open-circuit, and the 10 kΩ load takes 10/12 of this: v_out ≈ 278v_s. In dB: 20 log₁₀ 278 ≈ 48.9 dB. An unloaded cascade would give 20 × 20 = 400 (52 dB). The gain is lower because part of each stage's output voltage is dropped across its own output resistance when current flows into the next stage or load.

questions.q: Which dopant would make silicon n-type?
questions.why: A group V atom such as phosphorus has a fifth valence electron that is easily freed, so it donates electrons. Boron and gallium are group III acceptors (p-type); germanium is group IV, like silicon, and does not dope it.

questions.q: A silicon diode modelled with a constant 0.7 V forward drop is in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5 V supply, forward biased. What current flows?
questions.why: I = (5 − 0.7)/1000 = 4.3 mA. 5.0 mA ignores the diode drop; 5.7 mA adds it; 0.7 mA divides the diode drop by the resistance.

questions.q: Explain how a depletion region forms at a p-n junction and why the junction conducts much more readily in one direction than the other.
markScheme: Majority carriers diffuse across the junction (holes into n, electrons into p) and recombine
This leaves fixed ionised dopants: negative acceptors on the p side, positive donors on the n side, forming the depletion region with no mobile carriers
The fixed charge creates an electric field and built-in potential barrier that balances further diffusion in equilibrium
Forward bias lowers the barrier, so majority-carrier diffusion current rises exponentially (I ≈ I_s exp(V/nV_T))
Reverse bias raises the barrier and widens the depletion region; only a tiny minority-carrier saturation current flows until breakdown
questions.modelAnswer: When p-type and n-type silicon meet, holes diffuse from the p side (where they are plentiful) into the n side, and electrons diffuse from the n side into the p side, where they recombine with the majority carriers. This uncovers fixed ionised dopant atoms near the junction: negatively charged acceptors on the p side and positively charged donors on the n side. The resulting layer has no mobile carriers, so it is called the depletion region. The fixed charges set up an electric field pointing from n to p and a built-in potential barrier, which in equilibrium exactly balances the tendency to diffuse. Under forward bias (p side made positive), the external voltage opposes the built-in potential and lowers the barrier, so large numbers of majority carriers diffuse across and the current rises exponentially with voltage. Under reverse bias the barrier is raised and the depletion region widens; majority carriers cannot cross, and only a tiny reverse saturation current of thermally generated minority carriers flows, until a large reverse voltage causes breakdown.

questions.q: An n-channel MOSFET has K = 1 mA/V² and V_T = 1 V, with V_GS = 3 V, V_DD = 15 V and R_D = 2 kΩ. What are I_D and V_DS?
questions.why: In saturation I_D = K(V_GS − V_T)² = 1 × 2² = 4 mA, so V_DS = 15 − 4 × 2 = 7 V, which is ≥ V_GS − V_T = 2 V, confirming saturation. 15 V ignores the drop across R_D; 9 mA uses V_GS² and gives an impossible negative V_DS; 2 mA omits the square.

questions.q: For an n-channel enhancement MOSFET with V_GS > V_T, what condition places it in the saturation region?
questions.why: Saturation needs the channel pinched off at the drain end, which happens when V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T. V_DS < V_GS − V_T is the triode region; V_GS < V_T is cut-off; V_DS = 0 gives zero drain current.

questions.q: Describe how an n-channel enhancement MOSFET works, sketch (in words) its output characteristics, and explain how a load line is used to find the operating point of a common-source stage.
markScheme: Structure: n⁺ source and drain in p-type body, gate insulated by oxide; no channel when V_GS < V_T
V_GS > V_T attracts electrons to form an inversion n-channel; gate draws no DC current, so control is by voltage
Output characteristics: I_D against V_DS for several V_GS; linear (triode) rise then nearly flat saturation, with saturation current K(V_GS − V_T)² increasing with V_GS
Load line from KVL: V_DS = V_DD − I_D R_D, intercepts (V_DD, 0) and (0, V_DD/R_D)
Operating point where the load line crosses the curve for the bias V_GS; moving along the line shows the signal swing and its limits
questions.modelAnswer: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has heavily doped n-type source and drain regions in a p-type body, with a gate electrode separated from the body by a thin oxide. With V_GS below the threshold V_T, source and drain are isolated by the p-type body and no drain current flows. When V_GS exceeds V_T, the gate's field attracts electrons to the surface, forming an inverted n-type channel joining source to drain; the larger V_GS, the more conductive the channel. Because the gate is insulated it takes no DC current, so the device is voltage-controlled. The output characteristics plot I_D against V_DS for a set of V_GS values: each curve rises roughly linearly at small V_DS (triode region, behaving like a resistor), then bends over and becomes nearly flat once V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T (saturation), at a level K(V_GS − V_T)² that increases with V_GS. In a common-source stage, KVL round the drain circuit gives V_DS = V_DD − I_D R_D. Drawn on the characteristics, this is a straight load line from (V_DD, 0) to (0, V_DD/R_D). The quiescent operating point is where it crosses the curve for the bias value of V_GS. As the input signal varies V_GS, the operating point slides along the load line, which shows graphically the output voltage swing, the gain, and where the output will clip by entering cut-off or the triode region.

questions.q: A MOSFET in saturation has K = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V and V_GS = 3 V. What is its transconductance g_m?
questions.why: g_m = 2K(V_GS − V_T) = 2 × 1 × 2 = 4 mA/V (equivalently 2√(K I_D) = 2√4 = 4 mA/V). 2 mA/V omits the factor 2; 8 mA/V is 2K(V_GS − V_T)², keeping the square (equivalently 2I_D without dividing by V_GS − V_T); 1 mA/V is just K.

questions.q: A common-source amplifier has g_m = 4 mA/V, R_D = 2 kΩ, very large r_ds and no external load. What is its mid-band voltage gain?
questions.why: A_v = −g_m R_D = −4 × 10⁻³ × 2000 = −8; the common-source stage inverts the signal. +8 misses the inversion; −0.5 and −2 come from dividing instead of multiplying (R_D/g_m = 2/4 and g_m/R_D = 4/2 in kΩ and mA/V); halving g_m would give −4, not −2.

questions.q: A common-source amplifier has V_DD = 15 V, R_D = 2 kΩ and a MOSFET with K = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V and r_ds = 50 kΩ, biased at V_GS = 3 V. Draw (describe) the small-signal equivalent circuit and find the mid-band voltage gain with no load and with a 2 kΩ load capacitively coupled to the drain.
markScheme: DC: I_D = K(V_GS − V_T)² = 4 mA, V_DS = 7 V ≥ 2 V so saturated
g_m = 2K(V_GS − V_T) = 4 mA/V
Equivalent circuit: gate open; g_m v_gs current source with r_ds from drain to source; R_D from drain to signal earth (V_DD earthed)
With 2 kΩ load: r_ds ∥ R_D ∥ R_L ≈ 0.980 kΩ, so A_v ≈ −3.9
questions.modelAnswer: First the DC operating point: I_D = K(V_GS − V_T)² = 1 × 2² = 4 mA, so V_DS = 15 − 4 × 2 = 7 V. This exceeds V_GS − V_T = 2 V, so the MOSFET is in saturation and the small-signal model applies. g_m = 2K(V_GS − V_T) = 4 mA/V. In the small-signal circuit the gate–source port is an open circuit carrying v_gs = v_in; between drain and source (earth) is a dependent current source g_m v_gs in parallel with r_ds = 50 kΩ; R_D connects the drain to V_DD, which is signal earth, so R_D also appears from drain to earth. With no load, v_out = −g_m v_gs (r_ds ∥ R_D); r_ds ∥ R_D = 50 × 2/52 ≈ 1.923 kΩ, so A_v ≈ −4 × 1.923 ≈ −7.7. With a 2 kΩ load coupled through a large capacitor (a short at mid-band), the drain sees 1.923 kΩ ∥ 2 kΩ ≈ 0.980 kΩ, so A_v ≈ −3.9. The load roughly halves the gain, showing why a buffer stage is often needed.

questions.q: An inverting op-amp amplifier has R₁ = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ. What is its voltage gain?
questions.why: For the inverting configuration the gain is −R_f/R₁ = −10. +11 is the non-inverting gain with the same resistors; −11 and +10 mix up the two formulas.

questions.q: Why does the gain of a non-inverting op-amp amplifier hardly depend on the op-amp's open-loop gain A?
options: Because with negative feedback the gain A/(1 + Aβ) tends to 1/β when Aβ ≫ 1
Because the inputs draw infinite current
Because the output resistance is very high
Because the open-loop gain is exactly 1
questions.why: The closed-loop gain is A/(1 + Aβ); when Aβ is very large this tends to 1/β = 1 + R_f/R₁, set only by resistors. Ideal inputs draw no current (not infinite); ideal output resistance is zero, not high; open-loop gain is very large, not 1.

questions.q: Using the ideal op-amp rules, derive the output of a summing amplifier with inputs v₁ through R₁ = 10 kΩ and v₂ through R₂ = 20 kΩ, feedback resistor R_f = 40 kΩ and non-inverting input earthed. Evaluate v_out for v₁ = 0.5 V and v₂ = −1 V.
markScheme: Negative feedback and v₊ = 0, so v₋ = 0 (virtual earth)
No current into the inverting input: KCL v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂ + v_out/R_f = 0
v_out = −R_f(v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂) = −(4v₁ + 2v₂)
v_out = 0 V
questions.modelAnswer: With negative feedback through R_f and the non-inverting input earthed, the ideal rules give v₋ = v₊ = 0: the inverting input is a virtual earth. No current flows into the op-amp input, so KCL at the inverting node gives v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂ + v_out/R_f = 0. Hence v_out = −R_f(v₁/R₁ + v₂/R₂) = −(40/10)v₁ − (40/20)v₂ = −(4v₁ + 2v₂). With v₁ = 0.5 V and v₂ = −1 V: v_out = −(2 − 2) = 0 V. The circuit forms a weighted sum, so the two inputs exactly cancel here.

questions.q: A load takes 10 A from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. What capacitance in parallel would raise the power factor to unity?
questions.why: S = 2300 VA, P = 1840 W, Q = 1380 VAr. The capacitor must supply 1380 VAr: C = Q/(V²ω) = 1380/(230² × 314.2) ≈ 83 µF. 47 µF only corrects to 0.95; 111 µF uses the real power P and 138 µF the apparent power S instead of Q.

questions.q: With complex power defined as S = VI*, which statement is correct for an inductive load?
options: It absorbs positive reactive power and has a lagging power factor
It absorbs negative reactive power and has a leading power factor
Its real power equals its apparent power
questions.why: For an inductive load the current lags the voltage, so Q = VI sin φ is positive and the power factor is lagging. Capacitive loads have negative Q and leading power factor; only a purely resistive load has Q = 0 and P = S.

questions.q: Two loads are connected in parallel to a 230 V supply: load A takes 2 kW at unity power factor and load B takes 3 kVA at 0.6 power factor lagging. Find the total real, reactive and apparent power, the overall power factor and the supply current.
markScheme: Load B: P = 3 × 0.6 = 1.8 kW, Q = 3 × 0.8 = 2.4 kVAr (lagging)
Totals: P = 3.8 kW, Q = 2.4 kVAr (add P and Q separately)
Power factor = 3.8/4.49 ≈ 0.85 lagging
questions.modelAnswer: Load B has S = 3 kVA at cos φ = 0.6, so sin φ = 0.8: P_B = 1.8 kW and Q_B = 2.4 kVAr (positive, inductive). Load A has P_A = 2 kW and Q_A = 0. Real and reactive powers add: P = 3.8 kW and Q = 2.4 kVAr. Apparent power S = √(3.8² + 2.4²) ≈ 4.49 kVA (note this is not 2 + 3 = 5 kVA). The overall power factor is 3.8/4.49 ≈ 0.85 lagging. The supply current is S/V = 4494/230 ≈ 19.5 A.

questions.q: A 10:1 step-down ideal transformer has a 2 Ω resistor on its secondary. What resistance is seen at the primary?
questions.why: Referred impedance = (N₁/N₂)² × Z_L = 100 × 2 = 200 Ω. 20 Ω uses the turns ratio instead of its square; 0.02 Ω divides by the squared ratio (referring the wrong way) and 0.2 Ω divides by the plain turns ratio.

questions.q: In a transformer's equivalent circuit, which element represents losses from hysteresis and eddy currents in the core?
options: The winding resistances R₁ and R₂
The leakage reactances X₁ and X₂
questions.why: Core (iron) losses are modelled by R_c in the shunt branch. X_m represents the magnetising current; R₁ and R₂ represent copper losses in the windings; X₁ and X₂ represent leakage flux.

questions.q: A 10 kVA single-phase transformer has a core loss of 100 W and a full-load copper loss of 200 W. Find its efficiency at full load (unity power factor), the load at which efficiency is greatest, and that maximum efficiency.
markScheme: Full load: output 10,000 W; losses 100 + 200 = 300 W
Copper loss ∝ (load fraction x)²; max efficiency when 200x² = 100
questions.modelAnswer: At full load and unity power factor the output is 10 kW. Losses are the core loss (100 W) plus the full-load copper loss (200 W), so η = 10,000/(10,000 + 300) ≈ 97.1%. Copper loss varies with the square of the load current, so at a fraction x of full load it is 200x² W while the core loss stays at 100 W. Efficiency is greatest when the variable loss equals the fixed loss: 200x² = 100, so x = √0.5 ≈ 0.707, i.e. a load of about 7.07 kVA. Then the output is about 7071 W and the losses total 200 W, giving η ≈ 7071/7271 ≈ 97.2%.

questions.q:
A common-source amplifier uses an n-channel enhancement MOSFET with K = 0.5 mA/V², V_T = 2 V and negligible channel-length modulation (r_ds → ∞). The supply is V_DD = 12 V. The gate is biased by a potential divider R_G1 = 800 kΩ (to V_DD) and R_G2 = 400 kΩ (to earth); the source is earthed; the drain connects to V_DD through R_D = 3 kΩ. The input signal is coupled to the gate through a 100 nF capacitor from a source of negligible resistance, and the output is coupled to a 6 kΩ load through a large capacitor.
(a) Find the DC gate voltage, drain current and drain–source voltage, and confirm that the MOSFET is in saturation. [6]
(b) Find g_m and draw the small-signal equivalent circuit. [5]
(c) Find the mid-band voltage gain (as a ratio and in dB) and the input resistance. [5]
(d) Estimate the lower −3 dB frequency set by the input coupling capacitor. [4]
markScheme: (a) V_G = 12 × 400/1200 = 4 V; no gate current, source earthed, so V_GS = 4 V
(a) V_DS = 6 V ≥ V_GS − V_T = 2 V, so saturation confirmed
(b) g_m = 2K(V_GS − V_T) = 2 mA/V (or 2√(K I_D))
(b) Equivalent circuit: input across R_G1 ∥ R_G2 to gate; gate–source open; g_m v_gs from drain to source; R_D and R_L from drain to signal earth
(c) A_v = −g_m(R_D ∥ R_L) = −2 × 2 = −4, i.e. about 12 dB (inverting)
(c) R_in = R_G1 ∥ R_G2 ≈ 267 kΩ
(d) High-pass corner f_L = 1/(2π R_in C) = 1/(2π × 266.7 kΩ × 100 nF) ≈ 6.0 Hz
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The gate draws no DC current, so the gate voltage is set by the divider: V_G = 12 × 400/(800 + 400) = 4 V. The source is earthed, so V_GS = 4 V, which is above V_T = 2 V. Assuming saturation, I_D = K(V_GS − V_T)² = 0.5 × (4 − 2)² = 2 mA. Then V_DS = V_DD − I_D R_D = 12 − 2 × 3 = 6 V. Since V_DS = 6 V ≥ V_GS − V_T = 2 V, the saturation assumption is valid.

(b) g_m = 2K(V_GS − V_T) = 2 × 0.5 × 2 = 2 mA/V (check: 2√(K I_D) = 2√(0.5 × 2) = 2 mA/V). Small-signal circuit: V_DD becomes signal earth and the large coupling capacitors become short circuits at mid-band. The input voltage v_in appears across R_G1 ∥ R_G2 (both now from gate to earth) and directly as v_gs, since the source is earthed. The gate–source port is an open circuit. From drain to source (earth) there is a dependent current source g_m v_gs (r_ds is infinite). R_D (from drain to the earthed supply) and the 6 kΩ load both connect from drain to earth.

(c) The current g_m v_gs flows through R_D ∥ R_L = 3 × 6/(3 + 6) = 2 kΩ, so v_out = −g_m v_in × 2 kΩ and A_v = −2 mA/V × 2 kΩ = −4. In decibels, 20 log₁₀ 4 ≈ 12.0 dB, with a 180° phase inversion. The input resistance is R_G1 ∥ R_G2 = 800 × 400/1200 ≈ 267 kΩ, because the gate itself draws no current.

(d) The input coupling capacitor and the input resistance form a high-pass section: v_gs/v_s = R_in/(R_in + 1/(jωC)) = jωCR_in/(1 + jωCR_in) (source resistance negligible). Its corner is at ω = 1/(R_in C), so f_L = 1/(2π × 266.7 × 10³ × 100 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 1/(0.1676) ≈ 6.0 Hz. Below about 6 Hz the gain falls at 20 dB per decade; the output coupling capacitor is stated to be large, so it does not affect this estimate.

questions.q:
A workshop is supplied at 230 V r.m.s., 50 Hz from the secondary of a 2300/230 V single-phase transformer, which may be treated as ideal except for an equivalent winding resistance of 0.05 Ω referred to the 230 V side. The workshop has two loads in parallel: a motor taking 4 kW at 0.8 power factor lagging, and a heater taking 2 kW at unity power factor.
(a) Find the total real, reactive and apparent power, the overall power factor, and the current drawn from the 230 V supply. [6]
(b) Find the capacitance that, connected across the supply, would raise the power factor to unity, and the new supply current. [5]
(c) Find the transformer primary current before and after correction. [3]
(d) Find the copper loss in the transformer before and after correction, and explain why the supply company encourages power factor correction. [6]
markScheme: (a) Motor S = 4/0.8 = 5 kVA, Q = √(5² − 4²) = 3 kVAr; heater Q = 0
(b) Capacitor must supply 3 kVAr: C = Q/(V²ω) = 3000/(230² × 2π × 50) ≈ 181 µF
(b) New current = P/V = 6000/230 ≈ 26.1 A
(c) Ideal turns ratio 10:1: primary current = secondary/10, i.e. ≈ 2.92 A before and ≈ 2.61 A after
(d) Copper loss I²R: 29.2² × 0.05 ≈ 42.5 W before, 26.1² × 0.05 ≈ 34.0 W after

(d) Explanation: same real power with less current reduces I²R losses and voltage drop throughout the network and frees VA capacity in transformers and cables; reactive current earns the supplier nothing
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The motor takes P = 4 kW at power factor 0.8, so its apparent power is 4/0.8 = 5 kVA and its reactive power is √(5² − 4²) = 3 kVAr (lagging, positive). The heater takes 2 kW and no reactive power. Adding real and reactive powers separately: P = 6 kW and Q = 3 kVAr. The apparent power is S = √(6² + 3²) = √45 ≈ 6.71 kVA, and the power factor is 6/6.71 ≈ 0.894 lagging. The supply current is S/V = 6708/230 ≈ 29.2 A.

(b) For unity power factor the capacitor must supply all 3 kVAr. A capacitor across V supplies Q_C = V²ωC, so C = 3000/(230² × 2π × 50) = 3000/(52,900 × 314.2) ≈ 1.81 × 10⁻⁴ F ≈ 181 µF. The real power is unchanged at 6 kW, so the new current is 6000/230 ≈ 26.1 A, in phase with the voltage.

(c) For an ideal transformer, I₁/I₂ = N₂/N₁ = 230/2300 = 1/10. Before correction the primary current is 29.2/10 ≈ 2.92 A; after correction it is 26.1/10 ≈ 2.61 A.

(d) The copper loss is I²R with I the secondary current and R = 0.05 Ω referred to that side. Before: 29.17² × 0.05 ≈ 42.5 W. After: 26.09² × 0.05 ≈ 34.0 W, a reduction of about 20%. The same real power is delivered in both cases; the extra current before correction carries only reactive power, which does no useful work on average but still causes I²R losses and voltage drops in every cable and transformer between the generator and the load, and uses up the VA rating of that equipment. The supplier is paid mainly for real energy, so reactive current costs it money without earning revenue. Supply companies therefore charge large customers for poor power factor or require correction, and correcting at the load (where the reactive power is needed) relieves the whole network.
